thread:
marta: heads up — ALB started removing a bunch of edge pods in us-west-2 after I rolled the egress-networkpolicy change. Targets show TCP RSTs from the LB and then immediate deregister. :frowning:

sam: hmm, RSTs from the LB? can you paste the logs / tcpdump?

marta: what I see in ALB target logs: `health check failed (connection reset)` and in pod tcpdump:
```
15:02:41.123456 IP alb-3.2.1.4.443 > pod-ip.10256: Flags [R], seq 0, win 0, length 0
15:02:41.123457 IP pod-ip.10256 > alb-3.2.1.4.443: Flags [S], seq 12345, win 64240, length 0
```
so LB is sending RSTs after the pod SYN.

naveen: two quick theories: 1) the egress policy is DROP-ing the return traffic (SYN/ACK) path because of wrong namespace selector, LB sees SYN then RST? 2) SNAT port exhaustion / conntrack eviction causing symmetric NAT mismatch and LB resets.

claire: did the NetworkPolicy deny egress to the loadbalancer subnets or to the node egress path? we changed the policy to default-deny-to-internet earlier today.

marta: policy applied to label `edge=public` pods only. I think it targets egress to 0.0.0.0/0 except allowed ports; ALB health checks are TCP on port 10256 to pod readiness port. I confirmed an allow rule for 443 -> nodeport but not for the ALB health ip range.

yoel: ALB health checks come from the ALB nodes' ENIs, not the client IPs. if the ALB IPs aren't whitelisted, return packets can hit iptables SNAT path and get weirdly rewritten. Also if iptables rule order changed during policy apply, it can start sending RSTs.

sam: can you confirm kube-proxy vs ipvs mode? we recently flipped a kube-proxy conntrack tuning flag on the edge fleet which could interact with new policy.

marta: kube-proxy iptables, conntrack max is high. I dumped conntrack while repro-ing and saw a bunch of CLOSE_WAIT entries and some ephemeral SNAT ports in reuse. attaching snippet:
```
# conntrack -L | grep pod-ip | tail -n 5
udp ...
tcp  ESTABLISHED src=pod-ip dst=alb-ip sport=10256 dport=443 ...
tcp  CLOSE src=pod-ip dst=alb-ip sport=10257 dport=443 ...
```
not super obvious.

naveen: quick mitigation options: 1) revert the policy, 2) add an explicit egress allow for the ALB CIDR range to pods, 3) set ALB health to use node port instead of direct pod port (temporary).

claire: let's push an explicit allow for the ALB health IP range to the policy (least risky). do we have the full ALB health CIDR list for the region?

marta: grabbed from AWS: `3.2.128.0/17` (example) — added a rule to allow TCP -> pod:10256 from that CIDR. applying now.

infra-bot: deploy started by marta at 15:12:08 — updated NetworkPolicy `edge-egress` in ns `edge-prod`.

marta: rolled policy — checking targets... ALB still showing some failures but overall registrations are recovering. I've also added a temporary annotation to the Service to prefer nodeport health checks.

yoel: follow-up: we should add an integration test that verifies ALB health IP ranges are allowed before policy promotion. also add a note to runbook: when ALB target deregistration spikes, check NP allowlist + conntrack exhaustion.

sam: +1 on runbook. also file a ticket to audit other namespaces for similar default-deny rollout gaps.

marta: will file. thanks all. :raised_hands:
